title: Selfie Tips: Angles, Light and Camera Settings That Work — cv.cm
description: Selfie tips that work on any phone: best angle and arm distance, facing a window, avoiding big-nose distortion, portrait mode, mirror selfies, timer and burst.
h1: How do you take a good selfie?
answer: Face a window or open shade so soft light falls on your face, hold the phone at arm's length slightly above eye level, and tilt your face a little to one side. Tap your face to focus, lower the exposure if your skin looks too bright, and take a short burst. For a better shape, prop the phone up, use the rear camera's 2x lens and the timer.

body: Most selfie problems come from distance. The front camera is a wide-angle lens, and your arm keeps it only about 40 to 60 cm from your face. At that distance your nose is much closer to the lens than your ears, so the nose looks bigger, the face looks narrower and the ears may disappear. It is not your face; it is the perspective.

The second problem is light. The light in most rooms comes from the ceiling, which casts shadows under the eyes and nose. The third is the angle: a phone held low looks up the nose and makes the chin dominant.
Fix those three things and nearly every selfie improves, on any phone.

ol: Stretch your arm fully. More distance means less distortion. A selfie stick of about 70 to 100 cm helps even more.
Raise the phone so the lens is a little above your eyes, then tilt it down toward you. This is the most flattering default for most faces.
Turn your head about 15 to 30 degrees away from the lens, and keep your eyes on the lens, not on the screen. Looking at the screen makes your eyes look down.
Push your chin slightly forward and then down. It sharpens the jawline and removes a double chin.
Relax your shoulders and keep the arm holding the phone out of the frame, or let it show naturally at the edge.
Try both sides. Most people have a side they prefer, and the light may be better on one side.

body: If you want less distortion than an arm allows, prop the phone on a shelf or a small tripod 1.5 to 2 m away, switch to the rear camera, choose the 2x lens or portrait mode, and set a 3 or 10 second timer. The rear cameras usually have larger sensors than the front camera, so detail and low-light quality are better too. For full workflows with a tripod and remote, see the self-portrait guide.

The easiest good light is a window. Stand facing it, about 1 m away, so daylight falls evenly on your face and makes a bright catchlight in your eyes. If the sun shines straight in, the light is harsh; close a thin white curtain or move to a window that does not get direct sun.

body: If the light behind you is bright, such as a window or the sky, the phone may expose for the background and leave your face dark. Tap your face on the screen; most phones then expose for it. If your skin looks too bright or too shiny, drag the exposure slider (the sun icon next to the focus box on iPhone, or the brightness slider on Android) down a little. Many phones also have a front flash that lights the screen white. Use it only in the dark; it is flat and harsh close up.

ul: Portrait mode: blurs the background and works with the front camera on many phones. It needs enough light and may cut around hair badly; check the edges and lower the blur if it looks fake. On iPhone, swipe to Portrait and tap the front camera button.

Timer: set 3 seconds so your hand stops shaking before the photo is taken, or 10 seconds to get into a group shot. On iPhone the timer is in the camera controls; on Android it is usually in the top bar or settings.
Volume button or gesture: press a volume button to take the photo, so you can hold the phone with a better grip. Some Samsung phones can take a photo when you show your palm, or with a voice command.
Burst: hold the shutter (or slide it, depending on your phone) to take many frames, then keep the one with open eyes and a natural smile.
Wide selfie: some phones have a button that widens the front camera view for groups. Use it only for groups, because faces at the edges stretch.

Mirror front camera: by default many phones save the selfie flipped compared with the preview. On iPhone go to Settings, Camera, Mirror Front Camera to save it the way you saw it. Text on a shirt reads correctly only when it is not mirrored.
Grid lines: turn on the grid to keep your eyes near the upper third and the horizon straight.

body: Clean the front lens with a soft cloth first. A fingerprint on the lens makes the whole selfie look foggy and gives halos around lights.
A mirror selfie shows your outfit and your whole body, so it uses the rear camera, which gives better quality than the front camera.

ol: Clean the mirror. Dust and spots are very visible in the photo.
Stand at an angle to the mirror, not square to it, so you do not block the light and the pose looks less flat.
Hold the phone at chest height, not in front of your face, unless you want the face hidden.
Use the 1x lens and stand far enough away to show your feet. Keep the phone vertical so the mirror's edges are straight.
Tap your reflection on the screen to focus on you, not on the mirror's surface.
Turn off the flash. It reflects straight back into the lens.
Check the background in the mirror: an untidy room, a window showing your street, or another person.

body: A small edit helps; a heavy one is easy to notice. Straighten and crop first, then brighten slightly, lower highlights if the forehead is shiny, and correct warmth if your skin looks orange under lamps or blue in shade. Some phones smooth skin automatically; look for a beauty or face setting in the camera app if you want to turn it down. If you add beauty filters, use a low setting and compare with the original. Eyes, teeth and skin pushed too far look artificial, and in some places heavily edited selfies are not accepted for ID or official photos.

For social posts, crop to the shape the platform shows: 4:5 or 1:1 for many feeds and 9:16 for stories. cv.cm's crop tool has these presets. If you post on public sites, consider removing location data first; cv.cm's exif tool shows and strips GPS from a photo in the browser.

body.note: No selfie is worth a fall or an accident. Do not take selfies on cliff edges, rooftops, railway tracks, roads, in moving traffic, or near wild animals, and never while driving or cycling. Stay behind barriers at viewpoints. Look where you are standing before you look at the screen.

body: Be considerate of other people too. In busy places, step aside so you do not block a path or a view for long. Check who is in the background before you post, and ask before you include strangers or children who are not yours. Some museums, religious sites and venues do not allow photos or selfie sticks; follow the signs.

faq.q: Why do I look different in selfies than in the mirror?
faq.a: Two reasons. The front camera is close and wide, so it enlarges the nose and narrows the face. Many phones also save the photo flipped compared with the mirror image you are used to seeing.

faq.q: What is the most flattering selfie angle?
faq.a: For most people, the phone slightly above eye level with the face turned 15 to 30 degrees to one side and the chin a little forward and down. Avoid holding the phone below your chin.

faq.q: Is the front or back camera better for selfies?
faq.a: The back camera usually gives more detail and better low-light quality, and its 2x lens avoids distortion. Use it with a timer and a stand or a mirror. The front camera is easier because you can see yourself.

faq.q: How do I take a selfie at night without it looking grainy?
faq.a: Face the brightest light source, such as a shop window or a street lamp, and hold the phone very still. Many phones use night mode with the front camera; hold still for the full capture. Avoid the flash unless it is fully dark.

faq.q: How do I stop my selfies from looking blurry?
faq.a: Clean the lens, tap your face to focus, and use a 3 second timer or the volume button so pressing the screen does not shake the phone. In dim light, move closer to a window or lamp.
